newsitem.title: Italy: Italian summit threat put heat on Chirac.
newsitem.headline: Italian summit threat put heat on Chirac.

text.p: Doubts expressed by French President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday about Italy's ability to join Europe's single currency almost wrecked plans for a summit with Prime Minister Romano Prodi later this week, political sources said.
"The Naples summit was about to be scrapped," one source told Reuters. Another said: "Prodi's line was either he withdraws or we cancel".

The sources said Prodi, charged with selling a tough "budget for Europe" to Italians, had been so incensed by Chirac's remarks that he had intended to pull the plug on the October 3-4 meeting in Naples unless the French leader rowed back.
Chirac later told a news conference he "ardently hoped" that Italy would be among the first wave of countries to join monetary and economic union (EMU) in January 1999.

"I believe the Italian government is fully determined to do everything, as it has shown in its budget, to be in the first wave of countries to join the euro. I ardently hope it will succeed," Chirac said in the northern French town of Arras.

Prodi had summoned the French envoy to Italy, Jean-Bernard Merimee, for an explanation of Chirac's initial remarks, which drew a stinging charge of meddling in Italian affairs from deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni.

Both Veltroni and Prodi had pointedly refused to confirm whether the summit, set to be dominated by the EMU issue, would go ahead as planned until Chirac issued his afternoon statement calming the diplomatic storm.
Prodi then told journalists in response to queries to confirm their hotel bookings in Naples.

Chirac had told businessmen in northern France on Tuesday morning: "Things are going to go pretty quickly now, on January 1, 1999, for some countries which will have made the effort to clean up their economic and financial situation...It may take a little bit longer for those who are further behind, like Italy."

The president also said France's textile industry had suffered more from devaluation of the lira, the British pound and the Spanish peseta than from southeast Asian imports, adding it was "quite obvious that the lira's movement is completely incompatible with a single European market, even if it has rebounded slightly recently".

The latter remarks on the lira echoed similar comments by Chirac on Monday which diplomatic sources said the Italian government had decided to ignore in order not to sour the mood between the two countries ahead of the Naples meeting.
One source said Chirac's decision to repeat them on Tuesday had "staggered" the Italian government.

Prodi, appointed in May, spoke after meeting Chirac last June of a "new period of Franco-Italian friendship" following a frosty relationship between the French president and Prodi's predecessor Lamberto Dini, who is now foreign minister.
Chirac last November abruptly cancelled a summit in Sicily with Dini after Rome criticised France's nuclear tests.

The latest spat comes when Prodi's government has to convince Italians, and parliament, of the need for a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) deficit-cutting budget next year to meet the economic terms for EMU entry.

The budget is almost twice as big as Prodi had anticipated and includes a one-off "tax for Europe" which his centre-right opponents and some economists have branded a recipe for recession and discontent.
